content: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines high-quality health services as those that are effective, safe, and people-centered. Effectiveness refers to the delivery of evidence-based healthcare services to individuals who need them. Safety involves minimizing harm to patients receiving care. To maximize the benefits of high-quality healthcare, services must also be timely, equitable, integrated, and efficient. Timeliness reduces waiting times and harmful delays for both patients and providers. Integration involves coordinating care across different levels and providers, offering a comprehensive range of services throughout a person’s life. Efficiency focuses on optimizing resource use and minimizing waste. High-quality HIV services require reliable, people-centered clinical care delivered across community and facility settings. These services should be integrated with other health services, such as maternal, newborn, and child health programs, and implemented at national, subnational, district, and facility levels. The delivery of such services depends on a robust health system foundation, including effective management, adequate funding, skilled human resources, reliable information systems, and the procurement of quality pharmaceuticals, devices, and laboratory supplies. National HIV programs must establish quality management systems with appropriate structures, functions, and processes to support the delivery of high-quality services. Quality management encompasses activities such as quality planning, assurance, and improvement. Quality planning involves setting objectives, selecting health personnel, allocating resources, and designing initiatives to enhance care. Quality improvement focuses on continuously enhancing performance through data-driven interventions and addressing gaps in clinical outcomes. This includes defining a package of HIV care services, integrating quality assurance and improvement into service delivery, and engaging communities to strengthen care quality. National quality policies and strategies should align with broader health system goals and support leadership by health authorities. Quality management strategies should address systemic factors, including external influences like food insecurity and social inequality, while fostering a culture of continuous improvement. Effective quality management requires a shift from linear approaches to understanding the complexities of healthcare systems, identifying key intervention points, and addressing unintended consequences. Community engagement plays a vital role in improving care quality. Community-led monitoring allows individuals affected by HIV to assess the quality, accessibility, and effectiveness of health services. This process involves data collection, analysis, advocacy, and collaboration with health officials to implement improvements. Community-led monitoring empowers patients to provide structured feedback and hold service providers accountable, ultimately enhancing health outcomes. Sustainability is critical for maintaining quality management systems within HIV programs, especially in the context of universal health coverage and global health goals. Existing quality improvement efforts have demonstrated positive impacts on clinical outcomes but require sustained resource commitment from health ministries. Strengthening local systems, infrastructure, and information systems is essential for scaling up quality management initiatives. This supports the goal of enabling all individuals living with HIV to initiate antiretroviral therapy regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count.
